proposals.relationship: Wiebe credits Hofstadter’s The Age of Reform with shaping his generation’s historical questions, techniques and model of inquiry.
proposals.evidence_note: Brinkley1985p462 quotes Wiebe’s1969 retrospective self-placement and explains organization-related groundwork for Wiebe’s interpretation. Tyrrell2018pp398/400 corroborates conceptual debt while distinguishing criticism of status anxiety. Attribution remains through named scholars; original1969review and full1955/1967books unread. Influence on questions/method does not imply agreement with Hofstadter’s conclusions.

primary_locators.passage: Wiebe’s quoted graduate-school encounter and model of inquiry.
Hofstadter influence and retained conceptual frame.

proposals.relationship: Wiebe’s interpretation replaces Hofstadter’s nostalgic old-middle-class progressives with a new middle class pursuing bureaucratic reform.
proposals.evidence_note: Brinkley1985p472 explicitly calls Wiebe an influential challenger and distinguishes purposeful future-oriented reform from nostalgic displaced elites.479n15 cites Search for Order166/passim and preserves a different1962business-leadership argument. Fresh Rodgers1982p118 and Tyrrell2018p400 reinforce the contrast, but their original existing pair is not duplicated. Hofstadter’s positive formative role remains; this is not rejection of all his history.

primary_locators.passage: new middle class ... fulfill its destiny through bureaucratic means.
status anxiety reaction but conceptual indebtedness.

proposals.relationship: Tyrrell traces Wiebe’s bureaucratic-modernization conceptualization to Weberian rationalization theory.
proposals.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation at Tyrrell2018p399 explicitly locates the origins of Wiebe’s conceptualization in Weberian theory of rationalizing bureaucracy, while preserving critics’ objections and the unfinished character of change. Brinkley1985p462 also calls the interpretation Weberian. No direct original Weber title, edition, personal study chronology or inevitable modernization law is invented. Tönnies is separately named and lacks endpoint.

primary_locators.passage: origins ... Weberian theory of a rationalizing bureaucracy’s emergence.
important Weberian interpretations by Wiebe, Hays and others.

proposals.relationship: Tyrrell identifies Charles and Mary Beard’s large-scale historical narrative as a rhetorical resource for Wiebe’s Search for Order.
proposals.evidence_note: Tyrrell2018p398 describes the subtle impact in rhetorical exposition, specifying coauthored The Rise of American Civilization and recalling its plot, scope and forward motion;408n4 points to Wiebe’s appreciation at Search303. Mary’s endpoint is available, Charles’s is not; both retain authorship and neither becomes sole origin. Named mediated rhetorical assessment, not independently read source303 or claim Wiebe adopted the Beards’ entire substantive interpretation. Tyrrell only wonders about Hartz, who is held.

primary_locators.passage: Charles and Mary Beard’s coauthored work; rhetoric, sweep and plot.

proposals.relationship: Wiebe invokes Arendt’s account of a nation’s consensual limits to distinguish nationalism from unlimited imperial expansion.
proposals.evidence_note: Own chapter1p7 running onto8 cites Arendt despite saying she is no friend of nationalism, as part of his argument that kin-based national community and imperial expansion differ. This is a particular conceptual resource, not broad Arendtian affiliation or agreement on all nationalism. Preview omits note14 and full bibliography; no exact original title, edition or translator supplied. No full Arendt original read.

primary_locators.passage: genuine consent ... cannot be stretched indefinitely; nation versus imperialism.

proposals.relationship: Wiebe questions Mosse’s characterization of racism as heightened nationalism within a broader criticism of treating nationalism as pathology.
proposals.evidence_note: Own chapter1pp3–5 names Mosse’s formulation and develops an objection to conflating nations with states and blaming nationalism indiscriminately for state violence. The arrow is Wiebe’s bounded interpretation/criticism of that formulation, not a fresh reading or final judgment of Mosse’s whole argument. Preview omits note6, so original work/edition not invented. Sheehan’s foreword separately lists Mosse with other nationalism scholars but does not establish a particular positive Mosse debt.

primary_locators.passage: Mosse formulation; nationalism as voodoo doll for states; step back and start over.

proposals.relationship: White challenges Wiebe’s portrayal of a weak laissez-faire state by emphasizing government intervention, delegated power and corruption.
proposals.evidence_note: Own answer in2017Stanford interview names both Hofstadter and Wiebe, then specifies tariffs, subsidies and social welfare alongside limited administrative capacity. Collective criticism retains both targets; dossier only proposes the assigned Wiebe pair. White’s account is attributed and not turned into a claim that Wiebe ignored every state action. Tyrrell2018p401 similarly qualifies Wiebe’s weak-state model but is a distinct critic; no full White or Wiebe monograph claimed read.

primary_locators.printed_pages: answer to “How was ... viewed ... interpretation different?”
primary_locators.passage: strong government; power without administrative capacity; private authority and corruption.
state coordination, land grants and tariffs underrated.
